issues.description: The central construct, "causal understanding," is operationalized as performance on 10 pairwise prediction items after task exposure. This assesses relative outcome prediction for specific stimulus pairs, but not necessarily an explicit causal model of the system. Participants could succeed via perceptual heuristics, memorized regularities from prior trials, or simple cue use. The measure also samples only the two author-specified dimensions, so claims about the absence of causal understanding are stronger than the measure warrants.
issues.quote: This allowed us to rigorously measure participants’ causal understanding of the system after they completed their 5 trials (Figure 1.E). Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.

issues.description: The theory condition differs from the configuration-only condition in two ways: participants both received a predecessor’s theory and had to generate/write a theory themselves before the understanding test. Any difference in post-task understanding could therefore reflect self-explanation or reflection induced by writing a theory, not transmission per se.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system. Participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed.

issues.description: The manuscript draws broad conclusions about the transmission of causal models, but the manipulation reduces a theory to a very short, formulaic written sentence. This is a narrow and weak operationalization of causal-model transmission, so null effects may reflect an impoverished communication channel rather than the irrelevance of theories.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.description: The paper makes causal claims that inaccurate inherited theories constrained exploration and affected later understanding, but theory content categories were not experimentally assigned. They emerged naturally from prior participants and are therefore confounded with chain history, predecessor skill, prior configurations, and other unmeasured features. These analyses support association, not causal effect.
issues.quote: Finally, we show that the transmission of these inaccurate theories constrains learners’ exploration and has downstream effects on their understanding.

issues.description: Participants in the theory condition received both the predecessor’s configurations/scores and the predecessor’s theory. Because theories were transmitted alongside concrete exemplars, any effect attributed to theory transmission is inseparable from the content and quality of inherited configurations. The design does not isolate the unique contribution of verbal theory.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations” treatment (n = 70), the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in the chain were provided to the next participant in the chain. In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.description: The manuscript treats wide, uncertainty-heavy intervals as showing that theory transmission had no noticeable effect. But the reported intervals are broad enough to include potentially meaningful positive and negative effects. Without an equivalence test, ROPE analysis, Bayes factor, or other formal null-support framework, the data do not justify a strong no-effect conclusion.
issues.quote: Results show that the average wheel speed increased at a similar rate in the "Configurations + Theory" as it did in the "Configurations" treatment (Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h, Figure 2.A) ... Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: The text states that the analyses do not support an effect of theory transmission on understanding, yet the reported Generation × Treatment interval for understanding excludes zero. By the paper’s own Bayesian interval logic, this suggests some positive interaction, so the narrative conclusion is inconsistent with the reported estimate.
issues.quote: participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment 95% CI: (-2.54, 0.31), mean = -1.14; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: Despite preregistration, the final model was selected after comparing multiple candidate models on fit to the observed data. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom, especially because the candidate models, comparison criteria, and decision rules are not reported in the main text.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.description: A preregistered analysis was abandoned after nonconvergence, and the authors switched to an aggregated-score analysis after inspecting the observed negative correlation pattern. This is a consequential analytic deviation that changes the substantive question being tested and opens the door to outcome-dependent analysis choices.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that inertia and centre-of-mass understanding scores were negatively correlated, yet then aggregates them into a single total score. When subcomponents move in opposite directions, aggregation is not a valid summary of understanding and can artificially produce a null result by cancelation.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated (Supplementary Figure 9 and Supplementary Table 7) ... As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score

issues.description: The understanding outcome is a small bounded count derived from 10 forced-choice items, yet it is analyzed with a linear model. A binomial or ordinal model would better reflect the data-generating process and respect the bounded/discrete nature of the score. Linear modeling can misstate uncertainty and allow implausible fitted values.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass. ... We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable

issues.description: Trials in which the wheel did not descend were assigned a speed of 0 and analyzed in a linear model with positive continuous speeds. Non-descent is a qualitatively different outcome from slow descent; zero-coding collapses a two-process problem (failure vs. speed conditional on success) into one distorted metric. A hurdle, two-part, or survival/censoring approach would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset. We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable

issues.description: Non-descending wheels produce no valid descent time, yet the manuscript handles these trials inconsistently across analyses: in one place the data are restricted to reduce their occurrence, and in another failures are coded as zero speed. This inconsistent treatment of effectively undefined outcomes complicates interpretation and comparability of results.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset. ... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.description: Neither data collection nor analysis was blind to condition. This matters because the experimenter manually positioned weights on the wheel and ran the physical apparatus. Even with automated timing, unblinded manual handling can introduce subtle expectancy or execution biases.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: No formal sample-size planning was conducted, and several exploratory subgroup claims rely on very small cell sizes. This is especially problematic for null-effect claims about treatment differences and for mechanistic interpretations based on groups as small as N=6.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31. ... The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (Figure 3D and H).

issues.description: The manuscript reports speed as 1 m divided by descent time, but the timing switches are described as 92 cm apart. Unless additional distance corrections are specified, this is an internal inconsistency that affects all reported speeds, payoffs, and optimization percentages.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations ... Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails

issues.description: The analyses are explicitly Bayesian, yet posterior intervals are described as confidence intervals in the Results. This is incorrect terminology and blurs the distinction between Bayesian credible intervals/HPDIs and frequentist confidence intervals.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences. ... Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02)

issues.description: All participants saw the exact same 10 test items in the same order. Without counterbalancing or randomization, item difficulty is confounded with serial position, and fatigue, learning, or strategy shifts across the test may bias the understanding measure.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report the priors, number of chains/iterations, warmup, convergence diagnostics, effective sample sizes, posterior predictive checks, or the criteria used for model comparison. These omissions prevent readers from evaluating model adequacy or reproducing the analyses from the paper alone.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.description: The study used only sex-segregated chains, yet the discussion claims the findings generalize to mixed-gender collaborative settings. That generalization is not tested by the design and is therefore unsupported.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.description: The title and framing make a broad claim about culturally evolving technology, but the evidence comes from young French university students optimizing one low-dimensional, feedback-rich wheel task. Extrapolation from this narrow laboratory paradigm to culturally evolving technology in general is too strong.
issues.quote: Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology ... we asked successive ‘cultural generations’ of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system

issues.description: The paper argues that causal understanding is unnecessary, but the discussion itself notes that participants showed nonrandom, apparently informed exploration and "appropriate intuitions" about acceleration. This suggests the study mainly shows that rich explicit verbalizable theories are unnecessary, not that causal understanding in any meaningful sense is absent.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that despite exhibiting poor understanding of the experimental physical system, participants did not randomly explore the parameter space. ... This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.description: To support the proposed mechanism, the authors created exploratory categories based on observed wheel-production patterns after seeing the data. These post hoc groupings were not preregistered and no formal inferential model is described, so the mechanistic interpretation is vulnerable to arbitrary categorization and small-sample instability.
issues.quote: To test this mechanism, we grouped participants who did not inherit any theory (i.e. from the “Configurations” treatment) into 3 categories: those who produced various types of wheels, those who only produced balanced wheels, and those who only produced unbalanced wheels.
